tool.name: Parse table row into workflow parameters
tool.description: Turn selected columns of a single table row into typed workflow parameters.

param.label: Input table
param.help: Table with a header row. Exactly one row of this table is parsed into workflow parameters.

param.label: Column delimiter
param.help: Delimiter used by the input table.

param.label: Data row
param.help: Which data row of the table to parse. 1 is the first row below the header.

param.name: column_name
param.label: Column name
param.help: Must match a header cell of the input table exactly (ignoring surrounding whitespace).

param.name: column_type
param.label: Column type
param.help: Type of the generated workflow parameter. Booleans accept true/false, yes/no and 1/0 in any case.

tool.help:
.. class:: infomark
**What it does**
This tool reads **one row** of a CSV or tabular file and turns the selected columns into **typed workflow parameters** (float, integer, text or boolean). Each output appears in the workflow editor as a connection point that can be attached to the input of a downstream tool, which makes the tool useful for parameter sweeps: keep one row per parameter set in a table and feed the workflow with it.
This is the generic counterpart of ``recetox-aplcms - parse parameters``, which hard-codes the recetox-aplcms column names and types.
Usage .....
**Input**
- **Input table**: a CSV or tabular file with a header row. - **Column delimiter** and **Data row**: how the table is read. Data row 1 is the row directly below the header. - **Column**: one entry per value to extract, given as a column name and its type. Column names must match header cells exactly (surrounding whitespace is ignored).
**Output**
One parameter per configured column, named after that column. Values are validated against the selected type and the tool fails with a message naming the offending column instead of coercing it. Booleans accept ``true``/``false``, ``yes``/``no`` and ``1``/``0`` in any case.
Limitation - fixed number of slots ..................................
Galaxy requires a tool to declare its outputs statically, so the number of outputs cannot grow and shrink freely with the number of configured columns. This tool works around that by declaring a pool of **@MAX_SLOTS@ slots** and hiding the unused ones with output filters, which has three visible consequences:
- At most @MAX_SLOTS@ columns can be parsed per invocation; configuring more is an error. - The connection points shown in the workflow editor follow the configured columns, so adding or removing a column can change which downstream inputs are available. - Slots are positional: configuring ``mz_tol`` as the second column gives it the second slot. Output names are therefore generic (``float_0``, ``boolean_3``, ...), while the human readable label is the column name.
